title: Hybridization Assays: Reverse Line Blots, HPV Hybrid Capture and Expression Arrays
summary: Explain why a reverse line blot is “reverse” and read a rifampicin line-probe strip, state what HPV hybrid capture can and cannot report, and interpret expression-array results with multiple-testing correction and qPCR confirmation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 70 Hits 1, 8, 10 and 11 and Traps 2 and 4. Checked against Morgan 2005, Ki 2013, Morey 2006, Noble 2009 and Katsuya 2025. The reviewer says genes with < 4-fold differences cross-validate inconsistently; Morey 2006 reports lower correlation generally below 2-fold, so the lesson uses the source’s wording. Not taught: Holm–Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg by name (not in the sources read).

objectives: Explain the reverse line-blot format and interpret a rifampicin line-probe strip.
State what HPV hybrid capture 2 detects and cannot report.
Distinguish FWER from FDR and explain why array findings need qPCR confirmation.

scenes.title: A strip, a plate and a chip
scenes.altText: Three results on the molecular bench (invented): (1) a TB line-probe strip with one wild-type band missing; (2) an HPV hybrid capture result “positive” — the clinician asks “Is it type 16?”; (3) a gene-expression array listing 1,200 “significant” genes out of 20,000, with many only 1.3-fold changed. Question token: “What does each result really tell you?”

cues.text: Three results arrive. A tuberculosis line-probe strip is missing one wild-type band.
An HPV hybrid capture test is positive, and the clinician asks whether it is type 16. And a gene-expression array lists 1,200 significant genes out of 20,000, many changed only slightly.
What does each result really tell you, and what can it not tell you?

props.label: What does each really tell you?

scenes.title: Who is labelled, who is fixed
scenes.altText: Two blot cards. Classic Southern format: digested sample DNA is transferred to the membrane and a labelled probe is added. Reverse format (line-probe assay): several oligonucleotide probes are immobilized on a strip, and the labelled (biotinylated) PCR product from the patient is hybridized to them; colour develops where it binds. Example: a rifampicin line-probe assay has 10 probes — 1 M. tuberculosis complex, 5 overlapping wild-type (S) probes over the rpoB hot spot, 4 mutation (R) probes. Over 95% of rifampicin-resistant strains have mutations in an 81-bp rpoB hot spot.

cues.text: In a classic Southern blot, the patient’s digested DNA is separated on a gel, transferred to a membrane, and a labelled probe is added.
A reverse line blot flips that: many probes are fixed to a strip, and the patient’s labelled PCR product is hybridized to them. Colour appears where it binds.
A rifampicin line-probe assay for tuberculosis carries ten probes: one for the M. tuberculosis complex, five overlapping wild-type probes, and four mutation probes.
They cover an 81 base-pair hot spot in rpoB, where over 95 percent of rifampicin-resistant strains carry their mutation.

scenes.title: Reading the strip; reading hybrid capture
scenes.altText: Line-probe reading: all wild-type bands present and no mutation band → rifampicin susceptible; any wild-type band missing → resistance; a mutation (R) band identifies one of the four common mutations. Meta-analysis (Morgan 2005): on isolates, sensitivity > 95% in 12 of 14 studies and specificity 100% in 12 of 14; directly on specimens, specificity 100% and sensitivity 80–100%. Hybrid capture 2 card: RNA probes for 13 high-risk HPV types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68) hybridize to sample DNA; DNA–RNA hybrids captured by antibody, signal amplified. It reports high-risk HPV present or absent — it cannot identify the genotype or tell single from multiple infections.

cues.text: Reading the strip: all wild-type bands present and no mutation band means rifampicin susceptible. A missing wild-type band means resistance, and a mutation band names one of the four common mutations.
In a 2005 meta-analysis, sensitivity on cultured isolates was above 95 percent in most studies, with specificity of 100 percent; on clinical specimens, sensitivity ranged from 80 to 100 percent.
Hybrid capture 2 uses a mixture of RNA probes for 13 high-risk HPV types. Hybrids of sample DNA with probe RNA are captured by an antibody, and the signal is amplified.
Because the probes are pooled, the result is simply high-risk HPV present or absent. It cannot name the type, or tell a single infection from several.

props.title: Reading the strip
lines: All WT, no R band → susceptible

scenes.title: Expression arrays: correct, then confirm
scenes.altText: Multiple-testing card (Noble 2009): testing 20,000 genes at p ≤ 0.05 expects ~1,000 false positives by chance alone. Bonferroni: significant only if p ≤ α/n — controls the family-wise error rate (FWER), the probability of even one false positive. False discovery rate (FDR): controls the expected proportion of false positives among genes called significant — less strict. Validation card (Morey 2006): qPCR is commonly used to confirm array results; correlation is lower for small changes (generally < 2-fold) and improves when array data are filtered for quality (fold-change, p-value). Back to the hook: strip → rifampicin resistance; HC2 positive → high-risk HPV, type unknown (a genotyping test is needed); array list → apply FDR/FWER correction and confirm key genes by qPCR.

cues.text: Test 20,000 genes at a p-value of 0.05 and about 1,000 will look significant by chance alone.
Bonferroni correction calls a gene significant only if p is at most alpha divided by the number of tests. It controls the family-wise error rate: the chance of even one false positive.
The false discovery rate instead controls the proportion of false positives among the genes called significant. It is less strict.
Array results are commonly confirmed by quantitative PCR. Agreement is poorer for small changes, generally under 2-fold, and better after filtering for quality.
Back to the bench: the strip shows rifampicin resistance; the hybrid capture result means high-risk HPV of unknown type; and the array list needs correction and PCR confirmation.

props.label: RIF-R · HPV type unknown · correct + confirm

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Hybrid capture types the HPV strain” (✓ pooled probes: present/absent only; genotype needs a type-specific test); “A missing line-probe band is a failed test” (✓ a missing wild-type band indicates a mutation → resistance); “Small array fold-changes are reliable” (✓ small changes cross-validate poorly; confirm by qPCR).

cues.text: Trap one: hybrid capture types the HPV strain. No: its probes are pooled, so it reports present or absent; typing needs a type-specific test.
Trap two: a missing band on the line-probe strip means the test failed. No: a missing wild-type band means the patient’s sequence differs there, indicating resistance.
Trap three: small array fold-changes are reliable. No: small changes agree poorly with quantitative PCR and need confirmation.

scenes.title: Reverse = probes stay home
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Reverse blot: the probes stay home and the patient visits.” Plus “Hybrid capture = a crowd photo: you know someone high-risk is there, not who.” Tokens: Probes on strip · Patient amplicon labelled · Crowd photo. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: in a reverse blot, the probes stay home on the strip and the labelled patient amplicon visits. And hybrid capture is a crowd photo: you know a high-risk type is there, not which one.
Where it breaks: other HPV assays do report types 16 and 18; line-probe assays miss mutations outside the probed region; and arrays have their own conventions for labelling.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Reverse line blot: probes fixed, labelled amplicon added · missing wild-type band → rifampicin resistance”, “HC2: 13 high-risk HPV, no genotype · arrays: FWER/FDR correction, confirm by qPCR”.

cues.text: A reverse line blot fixes the probes and reads resistance from a missing wild-type band, hybrid capture detects high-risk HPV without typing it, and array hits need multiple-testing correction and qPCR confirmation.

props.label: Reverse line blot: probes fixed · missing WT band → RIF resistance
HC2: 13 high-risk HPV, no genotype · arrays: FWER/FDR + qPCR confirm

explanation.what: Plain language: hybridization tests find a sequence by letting a matching probe stick to it; what you can conclude depends on which part is fixed and how many probes are pooled. Scientific terms: Southern blot, reverse line blot (line-probe assay), rpoB rifampicin-resistance-determining region, wild-type and mutation probes, hybrid capture, DNA–RNA hybrid, expression microarray, multiple testing, family-wise error rate (FWER), Bonferroni correction, false discovery rate (FDR), qPCR validation.
explanation.why: In a line-probe assay the patient’s labelled amplicon binds wild-type probes only where its sequence is unchanged, so a missing wild-type band marks a mutation. Hybrid capture pools probes for many types, so a positive signal cannot say which type bound. Testing thousands of genes produces many chance “hits”, so p-values must be corrected and key results confirmed by an independent method.
explanation.measure: RIF line-probe assay: 10 probes (1 MTB complex, 5 wild-type, 4 mutation) over the 81-bp rpoB hot spot where > 95% of resistant strains mutate; susceptible = all WT bands, no R band; resistant = missing WT band. Accuracy on isolates: sensitivity > 95% (12/14 studies), specificity 100% (12/14). HC2: RNA probes for 13 high-risk HPV types; no genotype, cannot distinguish single vs multiple infections. Bonferroni: p ≤ α/n (FWER); FDR: proportion of false positives among calls. qPCR–array correlation poorer for small (< ~2-fold) changes.
explanation.differs: Southern blot (sample DNA on membrane, probe labelled) vs reverse line blot (probes fixed, amplicon labelled); hybrid capture (pooled detection) vs genotyping assays; FWER (no false positives) vs FDR (controlled proportion).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: why “reverse”, interpreting a missing wild-type band, whether hybrid capture types HPV, Bonferroni vs FDR, and why arrays need qPCR confirmation.

questions.stem: On a rifampicin line-probe strip, the M. tuberculosis complex band and four of five wild-type bands are present; no mutation band develops. What is the interpretation?

options.text: Rifampicin resistance, from a mutation not covered by the mutation probes
options.rationale: Correct. A missing wild-type band indicates a mutation in that region; the R probes cover only the four most common mutations.
Incorrect. Susceptibility requires all wild-type bands present.
Incorrect. The complex band confirms M. tuberculosis; a missing wild-type band is a result, not a failure.
Incorrect. The complex band is present.

questions.stem: A cervical specimen is positive by Hybrid Capture 2. The clinician asks whether HPV 16 is present. What is the best answer?

options.text: HC2 cannot tell; a type-specific (genotyping) test is needed
options.rationale: Correct. HC2 pools probes for 13 high-risk types and reports only present/absent.
Incorrect. Any of 13 high-risk types can produce a positive.

options.text: No; HC2 detects only low-risk types
options.rationale: Incorrect. HC2’s probe mix targets high-risk types.

options.text: Repeat HC2 at higher stringency to identify the type
options.rationale: Incorrect. Stringency does not separate pooled-probe types.

questions.stem: An expression array tests 10,000 genes. Using Bonferroni correction at α = 0.05, what p-value threshold applies to each gene?

options.rationale: Correct. Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests, controlling the family-wise error rate.
Incorrect. That would yield about 500 chance false positives among 10,000 genes.
Incorrect. That divides by 10, not by the number of tests.

options.text: It depends on the proportion of false discoveries allowed
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes FDR control, not Bonferroni.
